name: Square and Cube Root Basics
description: Understand what square and cube roots mean and use the basic product and quotient root rules.
script_scope: Teach the chapter's definitions of square root and cube root as inverse operations of squaring and cubing. Use small perfect squares and cubes first, then introduce the two root properties explicitly stated in the chapter: sqrt(xy)=sqrt(x)sqrt(y) and sqrt(x/y)=sqrt(x)/sqrt(y) for suitable positive quantities. Include roots of ordinary fractions, simple decimals, products and quotients. Show learners how to check a square-root answer by squaring it and a cube-root answer by cubing it. A learner should be able to recognise whether a question asks for a square root or cube root, split a convenient product or quotient under a square root, and keep exact values when the roots are perfect. Do not teach extraction algorithms here; those belong to the factorisation and long-division subtopics.

name: Square Roots by Prime Factorisation
description: Find exact square roots by pairing equal prime factors.
script_scope: Teach the factorisation method used in the chapter: resolve the number into prime factors, group identical factors in pairs, and take one factor from each pair to form the square root. Start with integers such as the chapter's 6084-style example, then extend the same pairing idea to fractions and terminating decimals written as fractions when useful. Make the exponent logic visible: a perfect square has even counts of every prime factor. Include checking by squaring the extracted root and spotting an unpaired prime factor. A learner should be able to factor a number, pair factors without losing any, calculate the exact root, and explain why an unpaired factor prevents an integer square root. Keep 'what must be multiplied/divided to make a perfect square' for the perfect-squares subtopic.

name: Square Roots by Long Division and Approximation
description: Extract square roots digit by digit for large integers and decimals, including approximate roots.
script_scope: Teach the long-division square-root method shown in the chapter. Mark digits in periods of two from the units side; choose the largest first square; bring down the next period; double the current root to form the trial divisor; choose the next digit so the completed divisor times that digit does not exceed the current dividend. Continue until the remainder is zero or until the requested decimal places are obtained. For decimals, make an even number of decimal places when needed and group decimal digits in pairs. Include estimating non-perfect roots to a stated number of decimal places and using a given approximate root value to simplify related expressions. Also teach the chapter's digit-count fact for square roots of perfect squares. A learner should be able to set up periods correctly, generate each next digit, place the decimal point, and stop at the requested accuracy.

name: Perfect Squares and Nearest-Square Problems
description: Recognise perfect squares and find least additions, subtractions, multipliers or divisors that create one.
script_scope: Teach the objective patterns around perfect squares. Use factor exponents to recognise a perfect square and to find the least factor needed to multiply or divide a number so every prime exponent becomes even. Teach finding the greatest perfect square below a limit and the least perfect square above it; from these, find the least number to subtract or add. Cover counting perfect squares in an interval by identifying the smallest and largest integer roots in range, and selecting the greatest or least n-digit perfect square. Include simple last-digit checks used by the chapter's objective questions, while making clear that a permissible last digit is only a clue, not proof. Include decimal perfect-square recognition where the decimal can be written as a power-of-ten fraction. A learner should be able to choose the correct neighbouring square and explain why the required adjustment is minimal.

name: Simplifying Surds and Radical Expressions
description: Pull perfect-square factors out of roots, combine like surds and simplify nested radical arithmetic.
script_scope: Teach the radical simplification patterns repeatedly used in the chapter: factor a radicand into a perfect square times a remainder, use sqrt(ab)=sqrt(a)sqrt(b), and combine only like surds after simplification. Work from the deepest root outward in nested expressions. Cover expressions built from known values such as sqrt(2), sqrt(3), sqrt(5), or sqrt(15); simplify roots of products and quotients before doing decimal arithmetic; and use identities such as (a+b)(a-b)=a^2-b^2 when they appear inside a radical. Include checking by squaring a simplified positive radical when practical. A learner should be able to recognise a hidden square factor, reduce the radical, collect like terms, and avoid the false rule sqrt(a+b)=sqrt(a)+sqrt(b). Rationalising a denominator is reserved for the next subtopic.

name: Rationalisation and Conjugate Radical Forms
description: Remove radical denominators using conjugates and simplify paired surd expressions.
script_scope: Teach rationalisation at the level used in the chapter's solved examples and objective questions. For a denominator such as sqrt(a)+sqrt(b), multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate sqrt(a)-sqrt(b), using (u+v)(u-v)=u^2-v^2. Handle the corresponding minus case, simple 1/sqrt(a) denominators, and reciprocal conjugate pairs. Show how expressions like (sqrt(5)+sqrt(3))/(sqrt(5)-sqrt(3)) become a whole number plus a surd, and how paired conjugates can make a later square or sum collapse quickly. Include multi-term radical fractions only where the same conjugate idea is enough. A learner should be able to choose the correct conjugate, keep the sign straight, simplify the denominator to a rational number, and check that the transformed expression has the same value.

name: Root Equations and Missing Values
description: Solve equations containing square roots, squares, missing radicands and scaled root relationships.
script_scope: Teach the chapter's missing-value and equation patterns involving roots. Replace the question mark by a variable, isolate the square root where possible, then square both sides only after the radical side is alone. Cover unknowns inside a radicand, unknown divisors under a root, equations such as sqrt(A/x)=k, simple equations of the form sqrt(c+x^2)=d, and scaling relations where a known root lets a related root be evaluated. Include equations in which a square or square root is nested inside ordinary arithmetic and objective questions that ask for the missing perfect square. Emphasise substitution back into the original expression and the positive principal square root used throughout the chapter. A learner should be able to undo operations in the correct order and avoid squaring too early.

name: Infinite Radicals and Telescoping Root Patterns
description: Turn repeating radicals into equations and simplify root series whose middle terms cancel.
script_scope: Teach the repeating-radical and telescoping patterns shown in the chapter. For an infinite radical such as sqrt(k+sqrt(k+...)), call the whole expression x, use the repeated tail to write x=sqrt(k+x), square, solve the resulting quadratic, and keep the positive value that fits the radical. Cover the chapter's examples with repeated 1, 2, 3, or 6 patterns. For sums containing denominators such as sqrt(n+1)-sqrt(n), rationalise each term so it becomes sqrt(n+1)+sqrt(n), and show how alternating signs or adjacent terms cancel when the expression is arranged as in the source. Also use 1/(sqrt(n+1)+sqrt(n)) = sqrt(n+1)-sqrt(n) for telescoping sums. A learner should be able to identify self-similarity, create the correct equation, reject a negative root when the radical is positive, and expose cancellation term by term rather than guessing the pattern.

name: Square-Root Applications and Square Arrangements
description: Model rows, grouped collections and other word problems where a total is a square or involves a square root.
script_scope: Teach the application patterns represented in the chapter's objective questions without expanding into unrelated later topics. Cover square arrangements where the number of rows equals the number in each row, so total=n^2 and side count=sqrt(total); finding leftovers when a total cannot form a complete square; collections where each member contributes as many paise as there are members, again producing n^2; and short equations where a herd or collection includes a term involving its square root. Include the year-age pattern in which a person is x years old in year x^2, using a simple equation between birth year, year and age. Show learners how to decide whether the unknown is the side/root or the total/square, keep units visible, and verify the story condition after solving.

name: Cube Roots and Perfect Cubes
description: Find cube roots, recognise perfect cubes and make numbers into perfect cubes by factor grouping.
script_scope: Teach cube roots by the prime-factorisation method used in the chapter: factor the number, group identical prime factors in threes, and take one factor from each triple. Extend to simple decimal cube roots by rewriting with powers of 10. Teach that a perfect cube has prime exponents divisible by 3, then find the least multiplier or divisor that completes or removes incomplete triples. Cover the greatest four-digit perfect cube and nearby-cube adjustment questions. Include simple cube-root expressions and the chapter's rationalising-factor style question only through the identity a^3-b^3=(a-b)(a^2+ab+b^2) or the matching sum identity already used in the book; do not introduce broader surd theory. A learner should be able to group factors in threes, calculate exact cube roots, repair exponents to multiples of three, and check the result by cubing it.
